headline: A ship ran the Iran blockade. The US shot out its engine.
summary: The US military said Friday that an aircraft fired on the stern of the Pacific Archer, a Palau-flagged merchant ship, in the Gulf of Oman on Thursday. The ship had left the Iranian port of Bandar Abbas and tried to run the US blockade of Iran's ports. Its propulsion failed and the crew was unharmed. It is at least the 15th ship disabled since spring.
cover_answer: A line of warships. Nothing in or out of Iran's ports.
table_question: When is it fair to stop someone by force if they ignore a warning?

5-7.chip: Bring it up if it fits the day
5-7.script: The United States has warships lined up around Iran, a country far away across the ocean, so ships can't come and go from its ports. One ship tried to sneak out, and an American airplane shot at the back of it to make it stop. Nobody was hurt. It's like a goalie blocking the goal, and the grown-ups have it.
5-7.why: Only if they hear it. "Nobody was hurt" comes first, and the goalie makes the stop ordinary.
5-7.why_long: Nothing to raise with a five-year-old. If a warship is on the TV, they take one vivid feature for the whole event and read your face before your words, so the script leads with the crew being fine and hands them a goalkeeper. A blockade is a block; that is all the word has to mean today. Expect 'will they come here?' No. The ships are far away.

8-12.chip: Bring it up if it fits the day
8-12.script: Since April, US warships have blocked Iran's ports. On Thursday a cargo ship left Bandar Abbas and tried to slip through. A US aircraft fired at its stern and the engine quit; the crew was fine. Think of a goalkeeper: the ball stops, the player doesn't get hit.
8-12.why: Warnings, then the engine: a rule applied in order. The goalkeeper keeps the force on the ball.
8-12.why_long: At this age a child is testing whether a rule gets applied the same way each time. The chain is a blockade since April, a ship that left port anyway, warnings, then a shot at the engine, and the military's count of 158 ships turned back is the rule applied. Expect 'what if the ship had kept going?' The article answers from June: three sailors died.

13-17.script: Is firing on a cargo ship with civilians aboard the smallest force that works? This one was warned, and nobody was hurt. In June a strike like it killed three Indian sailors. Second: Trump calls this war "effectively over," and two carriers still enforce a blockade. What does over mean?
13-17.why: Proportion, then a word. Force against a warning, and "effectively over" against two carriers.
13-17.why_long: A teenager can reason about what is not in front of them, so the script asks for proportion: a warned ship, no one hurt, set against June, when a strike like it killed three sailors. Then a word to test, "effectively over," against two aircraft carriers. Let them make the case first. Expect 'why is the war still on?' The articles don't settle it.

5-7.q: Did the people on the boat get hurt?
5-7.a: No. The plane hit the back of the ship, and the crew was fine.

8-12.a: Warships around a country's ports so nothing sails in or out.

8-12.q: Why shoot instead of just stopping it?
8-12.a: It says it warns the ship first. If it keeps going, it fires at the engine.

13-17.q: Can the US just shoot at ships?
13-17.a: Part of a war that began in February. Ships are warned first.

13-17.q: Is the war over or not?
13-17.a: Trump says effectively over. The blockade and two carriers are still there.
